title: Palaver Sauce
author: Fran Osseo-Asare
desc: Two documented versions from one kitchen — and in the classic one the ground melon seed is added and then left to set for five minutes without stirring.
longDesc: Palaver sauce takes its name, by its own author's account, from the Palaver at Elmina, where the dish served took on the name. It is greens, fish, meat and ground melon seed in palm oil, and the published recipe gives two routes. The time-saving version simmers the greens fifteen minutes then cooks the agushi ten minutes covered without stirring. The classic version boils the greens about five minutes and then, once the agushi is in, simply allows it to set for five minutes. Not stirring is the technique in both. Beaten egg or mashed beans substitute for the melon seed.
ingredients: 1 cup grated tomatoes, or a 16 oz tin
Fresh or dried red pepper, to taste
About a square inch of salted cod
steps: Steam the stewing beef about 10 minutes in the cup of water.
Soften the onions and garlic in the palm oil.
Add the grated tomatoes and tomato paste and cook down.
Add the beef, the fish fillets, the smoked fish and the optional shrimp or salted cod.
Boil the greens about 5 minutes, then add them to the pot.
Add the ground agushi and allow it to set for 5 minutes — do not stir.
Simmer the greens in the pot 15 minutes.
Add the ground agushi, cover, and cook 10 minutes without stirring.
Season and serve with ampesi (GHA006) or rice.
chefTips: Do not stir once the agushi is in. Both versions say so in different words — allow it to set, or cover and cook without stirring — and it is the only way to get the melon seed to hold together.
The classic version boils the greens separately for about five minutes; the time-saving one simmers them in the pot for fifteen. The difference is colour: separate and brief keeps them greener.
Half a cup of palm oil to half a pound each of beef and fish is a moderate amount for this dish, less than the cup some kontomire stews use.
Beaten egg, or refried or mashed beans, will stand in for the melon seed — her own substitution, and useful if agushi is hard to find.
Three protein sources at once: stewing beef, fresh fish fillets and smoked fish. That layering is the point, not excess.
The quantity range on the agushi is wide — half a cup to a full cup — and it decides whether this is a sauce with clumps in it or a thick mass. Start at half.
Whether palaver sauce and kontomire stew are one dish is not settled by any source. This recipe uses frozen greens generically; the kontomire versions specify cocoyam leaves.
commonMistakes: Stirring after the agushi goes in.
Boiling the greens long in the classic version.
A full cup of agushi on a first attempt.
Leaving out either the fresh or the smoked fish.
Substituting another oil for palm oil.
sources: Adapted from 'Recipe #73: Palaver Sauce, 2 versions', betumiblog.blogspot.com. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Posted by Fran at 7:56 PM', timestamped 2011-07-04T19:56:00-05:00. BYLINE NOTE, and it applies to every Betumi entry in this collection: every post on that blog prints the byline as 'Posted by Fran' — FIRST NAME ONLY — and no post examined prints 'Osseo-Asare' or any fuller byline. The footer links 'Fran' to a Blogger profile. The blog is Fran Osseo-Asare's, founded in 1997, and betumi.com carries the site-level line 'Content/Images © Fran Osseo-Asare', so the attribution is secure even though the per-post byline is a first name. SINGLE-PASS on the quantities below.

Ingredients exactly as printed, and printed ONCE for both versions: ½ lb stewing beef; salt, begin with ½ tsp; 1 cup water; 2 onions (about 2 cups chopped); ½ cup palm oil; ½ lb fish fillets; 2 × 10-oz packages frozen greens; 1 cup grated tomatoes, or a 16 oz can; ¼ cup tomato paste; fresh or dried red pepper to taste; ½-1 cup ground agushi; 3 garlic cloves; 8 oz smoked fish; 1 Tbsp dried ground shrimp (optional); ~square inch salted cod (optional).

TIMES as printed: steam the beef about 10 minutes. TIME-SAVING VERSION: greens simmered 15 minutes, then the agushi 10 minutes covered without stirring. CLASSIC VERSION: greens boiled about 5 minutes, then the agushi — 'Allow it to set for 5 minutes'.

THE NOT-STIRRING INSTRUCTION is the shared technique of both versions and is the single most important step. It matches the clumping cue in the kontomire stew at GHA023, which comes from an entirely different source — two independent sources arriving at the same requirement.
ETYMOLOGY, quoted from the post: at the Palaver in Elmina the dish served 'took on its name'. Elmina is in the Central Region and is Fante territory — the basis for the community attribution above.
SUBSTITUTIONS for the melon seed, as printed: beaten egg, or refried or mashed beans.

PROVENANCE DETAIL from the post: the dish was prepared 'at Flair'. Flair Catering in Accra is Barbara Baeta's — Osseo-Asare's co-author on The Ghana Cookbook — which places this version in a named professional Ghanaian kitchen rather than a home one.

A SECOND ETYMOLOGY AND ORIGIN CLAIM, from Rosalind Cummings-Yeates, "Ghana's Kontomire Stew Stirs The Soul", The Takeout, 22 February 2021 — context, no recipe. It describes the dish as 'a scrumptious mix of cocoyam leaves, bitter melon seeds, and fish', says it originated from 'the meeting of Europeans and locals from the town of Elmina', and notes that 'palava' is slang for a fuss. The Elmina origin is therefore attested by two independent sources, which is unusually good for a dish etymology.

WHETHER PALAVER SAUCE AND KONTOMIRE STEW ARE THE SAME DISH IS NOT SETTLED by any source consulted, and the two are published separately here. This recipe calls for generic 'frozen greens'; the kontomire versions at GHA023 specify cocoyam leaves. Afia Amoako's recipe is titled 'Kontomire/Palava Stew', treating them as one; the Tasty Tom cookbook calls its version 'Kontomire Abom Sauce', which brings in a third name. None of these resolves it.
reheating: Gentle heat without stirring, to keep the agushi intact.
healthBenefits: Melon seeds supply plant protein, magnesium, zinc and healthy fats.
Leafy greens contribute vitamin A, vitamin K, folate and iron.
Three protein sources give a very complete amino acid profile.
Red palm oil provides provitamin-A carotenoids.
culturalNote: Elmina is where the Portuguese built their castle in 1482, and a dish named after a palaver held there carries that history in its name — palaver meaning a dispute or a fuss, from the Portuguese palavra. Whether the sauce was served at a negotiation or simply became associated with one, two independent sources put its naming at the same coastal town.
